explanations.A: Incorrect. Contingent immunisation is an active strategy with an immunisation floor. It demands continuous monitoring of the cushion and would be abandoned into a full immunisation if the cushion were lost, so it involves more management, not less.

subject: Portfolio Construction

stem: A portfolio of 52 million funds a liability whose present value at current immunising rates is 50 million, and the mandate is contingent immunisation. The manager's latitude is *best* described as:

options.C: active management may continue while the 2 million cushion is positive and must stop if it is lost.
options.A: active management must stop at once, because a surplus means the liability is already fully funded.
options.B: active management may continue indefinitely, because extending duration will restore any lost cushion.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 61 | Portfolio Construction

explanations.C: Correct. Contingent immunisation permits active management only out of the safety cushion, the excess of assets over the present value of the liability at the achievable immunising rate. If active losses exhaust that cushion, the manager must immediately immunise.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A surplus is what makes contingent immunisation possible in the first place; the whole point of the structure is that the excess above the immunising present value can be put at risk in pursuit of a higher return.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Extending duration is an active rate bet that can as easily deepen the shortfall as repair it. Once the cushion is gone the mandate requires immunisation, because there is no longer any surplus to absorb an active loss.

subject: Portfolio Construction

stem: A manager is asked to track a broad bond index of several thousand issues while accepting up to 40 basis points of annual tracking error in pursuit of a modest excess return. The mandate is *best* described as:

options.B: enhanced indexing, matching the index's primary risk factors while taking small controlled deviations.
options.C: pure indexing, holding every issue at its index weight so that tracking error is driven toward zero.
options.A: active management, running a duration position materially different from that of the benchmark index.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 62 | Portfolio Construction

explanations.B: Correct. Enhanced indexing keeps duration and the main risk factor exposures at benchmark but seeks a small edge from issue selection, sector tilts and trading; a tracking error budget of a few tens of basis points is characteristic of it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pure indexing accepts no deliberate deviation and would not be given a tracking error budget to spend. It is also barely feasible in a bond index of thousands of often illiquid issues.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Full active management is defined by a willingness to run duration and sector positions well away from the index, and it carries tracking error measured in whole percentage points rather than tens of basis points.

subject: Portfolio Construction

stem: A fixed-income manager decomposes the expected one-year return on a bond portfolio. The component that is *best* described as arising even if the yield curve is entirely unchanged is:

options.C: rolldown return, as the bond's price converges along a static upward-sloping yield curve.
options.A: the price change from an expected move in the benchmark yield, given portfolio duration.
options.B: the gain or loss on unhedged foreign holdings from the expected exchange rate movement.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 63 | Portfolio Construction

explanations.C: Correct. If the curve does not move, a bond still ages into a shorter maturity that is priced off a lower yield on an upward-sloping curve, and its price rises toward par accordingly. Coupon income and rolldown together make up the rolling yield.
explanations.A: Incorrect. This component is by definition the return from an expected change in the yield level, so it is zero when the curve is unchanged; it is the term through which the manager's rate view enters the decomposition.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Currency return depends on the exchange rate rather than the shape of the yield curve, and it can dominate or reverse the local-currency return of an unhedged foreign bond regardless of what rates do.

subject: Portfolio Construction

stem: A manager builds a two-bond barbell from a short bond with modified duration 2.0 and a long bond with modified duration 8.0, and targets a portfolio modified duration of 4.4. The weight in the short bond is closest to:
origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 64 | Portfolio Construction

explanations.C: Incorrect. 40% is the weight in the long bond, the complement of the correct answer. Putting 40% in the short bond would give 0.40 x 2.0 + 0.60 x 8.0 = 5.6, well above the 4.4 target.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 55% would give 0.55 x 2.0 + 0.45 x 8.0 = 4.7, which overshoots the target duration. Portfolio duration is the market-value-weighted average of the component durations, so the weight solves exactly.
explanations.B: Correct. Solving 2.0w + 8.0(1 - w) = 4.4 gives 8.0 - 6.0w = 4.4, so w = 3.6/6.0 = 0.60. The barbell holds 60% in the short bond and 40% in the long bond.

subject: Portfolio Construction

stem: A five-year bond currently yields 4.00%. The four-year point on the same curve yields 3.60%, and the bond's modified duration one year from now will be 3.75. Assuming the curve is unchanged over the year, the bond's rolldown return is closest to:
origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 65 | Portfolio Construction

explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.40% is the yield pickup from rolling down the curve, the difference between the five-year and four-year yields. It has to be converted into a price effect by multiplying by the bond's duration at that point.
explanations.A: Correct. As the bond ages into a four-year instrument it is repriced from 4.00% to 3.60%, a fall of 40 basis points, and the price effect is approximately -3.75 x (-0.40%) = +1.50%.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 5.50% is the rolling yield, the coupon income of roughly 4.00% plus the 1.50% rolldown. The question asks for the rolldown component alone, which excludes the coupon.

subject: Portfolio Construction

stem: A manager expects an unusually large move in interest rates but has no view on its direction, and must leave portfolio duration unchanged. The trade *most likely* to express that view is:

options.B: selling a bullet and buying a duration-matched barbell, which raises portfolio convexity.
options.C: selling a barbell and buying a duration-matched bullet, which raises portfolio convexity.
options.A: extending duration with long-dated bonds, which raises sensitivity to the expected move.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 66 | Portfolio Construction

explanations.B: Correct. For a given duration, a barbell has greater convexity than a bullet because its cash flows are more widely dispersed. Higher convexity gains more when rates fall and loses less when they rise, which is the payoff to a large move of unknown sign.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This is the reverse trade. A bullet concentrates cash flows near a single maturity and therefore has the lower convexity of the two at equal duration; buying it is the way to express a view that rates will barely move.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Extending duration is a directional bet that rates will fall, and it also breaks the requirement to keep duration unchanged. A large rise in rates would produce a substantial loss.

subject: Portfolio Construction

stem: A credit manager is comparing two bonds from the same issuer that differ in their embedded call features and wants a spread measure that is comparable across the two. The measure *most likely* used is:

options.A: the option-adjusted spread, which strips the embedded option's value out of the spread.
options.B: the G-spread, the spread over an interpolated government bond yield of the same maturity.
options.C: the I-spread, the spread over the interpolated swap rate at the bond's maturity date.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 67 | Portfolio Construction

explanations.A: Correct. A callable bond's quoted spread is inflated by compensation for the option written to the issuer. The option-adjusted spread removes the modelled option value, leaving the credit and liquidity compensation that is comparable across differing structures.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The G-spread is a simple yield difference over an interpolated government yield. It says nothing about optionality, so a callable bond will show a wider G-spread than an otherwise identical bullet purely because of the call.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The I-spread changes only the reference curve, from governments to swaps, and is often preferred for cross-currency comparison. Like the G-spread it makes no adjustment for an embedded option.

subject: Portfolio Construction

stem: A corporate bond trades at a spread of 200 basis points with a spread duration of 5.0. Over the coming year the manager expects the spread to widen by 10 basis points and expects credit losses of 30 basis points. The expected excess return over the year is closest to:

options.C: 120 bp
options.A: 150 bp
options.B: 170 bp

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 68 | Portfolio Construction

explanations.C: Correct. Expected excess return is roughly the spread earned less the spread duration times the expected spread change less expected credit losses: 200 - (5.0 x 10) - 30 = 120 basis points.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 150 bp subtracts the 50 basis point price effect of the spread widening but omits the 30 basis points of expected credit loss, which is a separate deduction for expected default multiplied by loss severity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 170 bp subtracts the expected credit loss but ignores the mark-to-market effect of the widening. A 10 basis point widening on a spread duration of 5.0 costs about 50 basis points of price.

subject: Portfolio Construction

stem: A bond portfolio has a market value of 50 million and a modified duration of 4.0. The liability it funds has the same present value and a modified duration of 7.0. A bond futures contract has a basis point value of 75 per contract. The overlay that *most likely* closes the duration gap is:

options.C: buying 200 contracts
options.A: selling 200 contracts
options.B: buying 467 contracts

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 69 | Portfolio Construction

explanations.C: Correct. Asset basis point value is 4.0 x 50,000,000 x 0.0001 = 20,000 and the liability's is 35,000, a gap of 15,000. Dividing by the 75 per contract gives 200 contracts, bought because asset duration must rise toward the liability's.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The contract count is right but the direction is wrong. Selling futures would cut asset basis point value to 5,000 and widen the mismatch, leaving the plan badly exposed to a fall in rates.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 467 contracts is the liability's full basis point value of 35,000 divided by 75, which ignores the 20,000 of basis point value the physical bonds already provide. Only the gap needs to be overlaid.

subject: Portfolio Construction

stem: An analyst produces three reports on the same equity portfolio: the first states the fund's time-weighted rate of return for the quarter, the second explains how much of the fund's 140 bp active return came from sector weighting versus stock picking, and the third explains how much of the fund's tracking error came from its exposure to the value factor. The second report is best described as:

options.C: return measurement, because it quantifies the return the fund actually earned.
options.A: return attribution, because it explains the sources of the realised active return.
options.B: risk attribution, because it decomposes the variability of the fund's active return.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 70 | Performance Measurement

explanations.C: Incorrect. Return measurement is the first report — the calculation of the return itself, time-weighted or money-weighted. It establishes what the return was, but says nothing about why it arose.
explanations.A: Correct. Return attribution is an ex post exercise that links the realised return, or the active return, back to the investment decisions that produced it, typically allocation and selection.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Risk attribution is the third report. It decomposes the variability of return — total risk for an absolute mandate, active risk for a benchmark-relative one — rather than the return itself.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: A portfolio holds 30% in the energy sector against a benchmark weight of 20%. Over the period the energy segment of the benchmark returned 8.0%, the portfolio's own energy holdings returned 11.0%, and the total benchmark returned 5.0%. Using the Brinson-Fachler model, the allocation effect contributed by the energy sector is closest to:
origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 71 | Performance Measurement

explanations.C: Correct. Brinson-Fachler allocation is (wP − wB)(RB,sector − RB,total) = (0.30 − 0.20)(8.0% − 5.0%) = 0.10 × 3.0% = 0.30%. The overweight is credited only with the sector's outperformance of the whole benchmark.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.60% is the selection effect, wB(RP,sector − RB,sector) = 0.20 × (11.0% − 8.0%). That measures stock picking inside energy, not the decision to overweight the sector.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 0.80% is the Brinson-Hood-Beebower allocation effect, (wP − wB) × RB,sector = 0.10 × 8.0%, which measures the overweight against a return of zero instead of against the benchmark return.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: A portfolio holds 40% in industrials against a benchmark weight of 25%. The portfolio's industrials holdings returned 6.0% while the industrials segment of the benchmark returned 10.0%, and the total benchmark returned 4.0%. In a three-factor Brinson attribution, the interaction effect for industrials is closest to:
origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 72 | Performance Measurement

explanations.B: Incorrect. −1.60% is selection measured at the portfolio weight, wP(RP − RB) = 0.40 × (−4.0%). That is the two-factor form, which absorbs interaction into selection rather than reporting it separately.
explanations.C: Incorrect. −1.00% is the selection effect, wB(RP − RB) = 0.25 × (−4.0%). It isolates the picking decision at the benchmark weight and deliberately excludes the effect of the overweight.
explanations.A: Correct. Interaction is (wP − wB)(RP,sector − RB,sector) = (0.40 − 0.25)(6.0% − 10.0%) = 0.15 × (−4.0%) = −0.60%. It is negative because the manager overweighted a sector in which its selection was poor, so the two decisions compounded against it.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: In the Brinson-Fachler model the allocation effect for a segment is the active weight multiplied by the segment's benchmark return less the total benchmark return, rather than by the segment's benchmark return alone. This adjustment is most likely made because it:

options.C: rewards an overweight only when the segment outperforms the overall benchmark.
options.A: rewards an overweight whenever the segment's own benchmark return is positive.
options.B: removes the interaction term by assigning it entirely to the selection effect.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 73 | Performance Measurement

explanations.C: Correct. Netting off the total benchmark return makes allocation measure the weighting decision itself. Overweighting a segment that returned 3% in a benchmark that returned 5% destroyed value, and Brinson-Fachler records that correctly as a negative allocation effect.
explanations.A: Incorrect. That describes the Brinson-Hood-Beebower specification, which measures the segment return against zero. In a strongly rising market it credits almost every overweight, even one to a segment that badly lagged the benchmark.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Whether interaction is reported separately or folded into selection is the choice between a three-factor and a two-factor attribution. It is a separate decision from how the allocation term is benchmarked.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: A portfolio returned 21.0% over a year in which its benchmark returned 10.0%. Measured geometrically, the portfolio's excess return over the benchmark is closest to:
origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 74 | Performance Measurement

explanations.C: Incorrect. 9.1% divides the arithmetic excess return by one plus the portfolio return, 11.0%/1.21. The geometric measure deflates by the benchmark's wealth relative, not by the portfolio's.
explanations.A: Correct. The geometric excess return is (1 + RP)/(1 + RB) − 1 = 1.21/1.10 − 1 = 10.0%. Being a ratio of wealth relatives, single-period geometric excess returns chain by multiplication, so they compound cleanly across periods.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 11.0% is the arithmetic excess return, RP − RB. Arithmetic excess returns do not sum to the multi-period excess return, which is why multi-period arithmetic attribution needs a smoothing adjustment.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: An asset owner receives a manager's monthly returns but is contractually unable to obtain either the manager's holdings or its trade records. The attribution method the asset owner can still apply is most likely:

options.C: returns-based attribution, which regresses the return series on a set of factor returns.
options.A: holdings-based attribution, which revalues the beginning-of-period positions each period.
options.B: transaction-based attribution, which combines the holdings with the trades placed intraperiod.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 75 | Performance Measurement

explanations.C: Correct. Returns-based attribution needs only the portfolio's return series and a set of explanatory index or factor returns. It is the least data-intensive method and the only one that survives when holdings are withheld, at the cost of being the least precise.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Holdings-based attribution requires the positions held at the start of each subperiod. It is more precise than a returns-based method, but it is unavailable without position data and it still misses the effect of trading within the period.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Transaction-based attribution is the most accurate of the three because it uses both the holdings and every trade, so it reconciles exactly to the portfolio's return. It also carries by far the heaviest data requirement.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: A fixed-income attribution report covering a quarter in which the yield curve steepened shows a large positive contribution from the portfolio's shorter-than-benchmark duration and a small negative contribution from its underweight to BBB rated issuers. These two contributions are best classified, respectively, as:

options.A: a yield-curve effect and a spread effect.
options.B: a spread effect and a selection effect.
options.C: a selection effect and a yield-curve effect.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 76 | Performance Measurement

explanations.A: Correct. Duration and curve positioning are captured by the yield-curve (interest rate) effect, while the return earned from positioning across credit-quality or spread sectors is captured by the spread effect.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The spread effect captures credit positioning, not duration. The selection effect is the residual attributable to choosing individual bonds within a sector, once the curve and spread effects have been removed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Selection measures the value added by picking particular securities inside a segment. A portfolio-level duration stance is a curve decision, and a credit-quality underweight is a spread decision.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: A benchmark-relative equity manager's risk model reports that the factor component of its active risk is 3.2% and the asset-specific component is 2.4%, and that the two components are uncorrelated. The manager's total active risk is closest to:
origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 77 | Performance Measurement

explanations.A: Correct. Uncorrelated components add in variance, not in standard deviation: 3.2² + 2.4² = 10.24 + 5.76 = 16.0, and the square root of 16.0 is 4.0%. A benchmark-relative mandate decomposes active risk this way; an absolute-return mandate decomposes total portfolio variance instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 5.6% simply adds the two standard deviations together. That result would hold only if the factor and specific components were perfectly correlated, which the risk model has explicitly ruled out.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 16.0 is the active variance expressed in squared percent, not a risk figure. It has to be converted back to a standard deviation before it can be compared with a tracking-error budget.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: A plan sponsor proposes to evaluate a newly hired manager against the median return of a universe of peer managers pursuing a similar strategy. Of the properties of a valid benchmark, the one this proposal most clearly fails is that a benchmark should be:

options.A: measurable, because a peer universe's periodic return cannot be calculated.
options.B: investable, because the median peer manager cannot be held as an alternative.
options.C: appropriate, because peer universes are drawn from a different asset class.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 78 | Performance Measurement

explanations.A: Incorrect. The universe's return can in fact be computed once the peers have reported, so measurability is not the sharpest objection. The deeper problem is that the number exists only after the fact and cannot be replicated.
explanations.B: Correct. A valid benchmark has to be a genuine passive alternative the investor could have held instead. The median manager is identifiable only in hindsight, its holdings are unpublished, and the universe is survivorship-biased, so it can never be bought.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A peer universe is normally assembled precisely from managers in the same asset class and style, so appropriateness is usually the property it comes closest to satisfying, not the one it fails.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: A plan sponsor measures its total equity programme against a broad market index, while each underlying manager is measured against its own custom style benchmark. The difference in return between the aggregate of the managers' style benchmarks and the broad market index is best described as:

options.A: misfit return, arising from the style composition of the manager line-up.
options.B: true active return, arising from each manager's deviation from its own benchmark.
options.C: specific return, arising from stock-level risk the sponsor's factor model omits.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 79 | Performance Measurement

explanations.A: Correct. Total active return splits into true active return — each manager against its own normal portfolio — and misfit return, the aggregate of those normal portfolios against the sponsor's policy benchmark. Misfit belongs to the sponsor's structure decision, not to manager skill.
explanations.B: Incorrect. True active return is measured against each manager's own style benchmark and is what a manager should be held accountable for. It reveals nothing about whether the sponsor assembled the right mix of styles.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Specific, or idiosyncratic, return is the part of one portfolio's return that common factors do not explain. It is a component within a portfolio, not a gap between two different benchmarks.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: An individual investor will place her entire investable wealth with a single manager and will hold nothing else alongside it. In appraising the candidate managers, the most appropriate risk-adjusted measure is most likely the:

options.A: Sharpe ratio, because the investor is exposed to the manager's total risk.
options.B: Treynor ratio, because only systematic risk is compensated in equilibrium.
options.C: information ratio, because it scales active return by the manager's active risk.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 80 | Performance Measurement

explanations.A: Correct. When the portfolio is the investor's entire holding, its diversifiable risk is not diversified away anywhere else, so the relevant denominator is total risk measured by standard deviation. That is the Sharpe ratio.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The Treynor ratio divides excess return by beta and is appropriate when the portfolio is one sleeve of a larger, well-diversified whole, so that only its contribution to systematic risk matters to the owner.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The information ratio divides active return by tracking error. It appraises a manager against a benchmark the manager is expected to track, not one who will constitute the investor's whole portfolio.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: Over the past year a portfolio returned 11.4% against a benchmark return of 8.4%. Its tracking error was 4.0%, its total standard deviation was 15.0%, and the risk-free rate was 2.4%. The portfolio's information ratio is closest to:
origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 81 | Performance Measurement

explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.60 is the Sharpe ratio, (11.4% − 2.4%)/15.0%. It divides excess return over the risk-free rate by total standard deviation, so it appraises stand-alone rather than benchmark-relative performance.
explanations.B: Correct. The information ratio is mean active return divided by active risk: (11.4% − 8.4%)/4.0% = 3.0/4.0 = 0.75. Numerator and denominator must both be measured against the same benchmark.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 2.25 mixes the two measures, dividing excess return over the risk-free rate by tracking error. The information ratio's numerator has to be the return over the benchmark, not over cash.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: A portfolio returned 12.8% while its benchmark returned 9.0% and the risk-free rate was 2.0%. The portfolio's beta is 1.20, its total standard deviation is 15.0%, and the standard deviation of its non-systematic (residual) return is 8.0%. The portfolio's appraisal ratio is closest to:
origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 82 | Performance Measurement

explanations.B: Incorrect. 0.16 divides alpha by total standard deviation. The appraisal ratio's denominator is non-systematic risk alone, because alpha is what remains after the systematic exposure has been paid for.
explanations.C: Correct. Jensen's alpha is 12.8% − [2.0% + 1.20(9.0% − 2.0%)] = 12.8% − 10.4% = 2.4%. The appraisal ratio divides that alpha by the standard deviation of the residual return: 2.4%/8.0% = 0.30.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 0.72 is the Sharpe ratio, (12.8% − 2.0%)/15.0%. It sets raw excess return over cash against total risk, so it does not isolate the manager's alpha at all.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: In months when its benchmark rose, a fund returned an average of 2.7% against the benchmark's 3.0%. In months when the benchmark fell, the fund returned an average of −1.5% against the benchmark's −2.0%. The fund's capture ratio is closest to:
origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 83 | Performance Measurement

explanations.C: Incorrect. 0.83 inverts the ratio, dividing downside capture by upside capture. Defined that way a lower number would signal the better manager, which is not the convention.
explanations.A: Correct. Upside capture is 2.7%/3.0% = 90% and downside capture is −1.5%/−2.0% = 75%, so the capture ratio is 90/75 = 1.20. A ratio above one shows the desirable convex asymmetry: more of the up is kept than of the down.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 1.80 divides the fund's own average up-month return by the absolute value of its average down-month return. Capture must be measured against the benchmark's up and down returns, not the fund's own.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: A plan sponsor hires a manager on the strength of a strong three-year record; the manager in fact has no skill and subsequently adds no value. Treating the null hypothesis as 'the manager adds no value', this outcome is best described as:

options.A: a Type I error, rejecting a null of no value added that was true.
options.B: a Type II error, failing to reject a null of no value added that was false.
options.C: sampling error rather than a decision error, given the short track record.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 84 | Performance Measurement

explanations.A: Correct. Hiring amounts to rejecting the null of no value added. The null was in fact true, so this is a Type I error, and its cost — fees and underperformance paid to an unskilled manager — is visible in the plan's reported results.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A Type II error is the opposite mistake: failing to hire, or firing, a manager who does add value. Its cost is foregone alpha, which is real but never appears in any performance report.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A short record raises the probability of both types of error, but it does not change how the outcome is classified. A hiring decision was taken and the manager proved unskilled, which is a Type I error.

subject: Performance Measurement

stem: A manager holds 10,000 shares bought at 44.00 and writes 100 covered calls, each on 100 shares, struck at 47.00 for a premium of 1.60 per share. Ignoring dividends and transaction costs, the maximum profit and the breakeven share price at expiration are most likely:

options.A: maximum profit 3.00 per share, breakeven at 44.00 per share.
options.B: maximum profit 4.60 per share, breakeven at 42.40 per share.
options.C: maximum profit 1.60 per share, breakeven at 45.40 per share.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 85 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.A: Incorrect. This counts only the 47.00 - 44.00 gain on the shares and treats the premium as irrelevant. The premium is received at inception, so it both adds to the capped gain and lowers the breakeven below the purchase price.
explanations.B: Correct. Above 47.00 the shares are called away, so the gain is capped at (47.00 - 44.00) + 1.60 = 4.60. The premium cushions the downside, so the position breaks even at 44.00 - 1.60 = 42.40.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The premium alone is the writer's maximum profit only when a call is written against cash rather than stock; here the shares also appreciate to the strike. Breakeven is set from the purchase price less the premium, not from the strike.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A portfolio manager holds a share trading at 82.00 and buys a three-month put struck at 78.00. The payoff profile of the resulting position at expiration is best described as equivalent to:

options.C: a long call struck at 78.00, reduced by the premium paid for the put.
options.A: a short put struck at 78.00, increased by the premium received for it.
options.B: a bull call spread with a lower strike of 78.00 and a capped upside.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 86 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.C: Correct. Long underlying plus long put is the synthetic long call of put-call parity: losses stop at the strike while the upside is retained, and the whole profile sits lower by the premium outlay.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A short put is the synthetic equivalent of a covered call, that is, long underlying plus a written call. That position leaves the downside open and caps the upside, the opposite of a protective put.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A bull call spread caps the upside at its higher strike, whereas a protective put leaves the upside unlimited. The two structures share only a limited downside, not their payoff shape.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A manager holds a share at 62.00, buys a put struck at 58.00 for 1.90 and writes a call struck at 68.00 for 1.40. At expiration, the maximum gain and the maximum loss per share on the collar are most likely:

options.A: maximum gain 5.50 and maximum loss 4.50.
options.B: maximum gain 6.00 and maximum loss 4.00.
options.C: maximum gain 6.50 and maximum loss 3.50.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 87 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.A: Correct. The collar costs a net 1.90 - 1.40 = 0.50, so the effective cost basis is 62.50. The gain caps at 68.00 - 62.50 = 5.50 and the loss floors at 62.50 - 58.00 = 4.50.
explanations.B: Incorrect. These are the raw strike-to-price distances, 68.00 - 62.00 and 62.00 - 58.00, with the net premium ignored. A net-debit collar shifts both outcomes against the holder by the amount paid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This adds the 0.50 net debit to the gain and subtracts it from the loss, the wrong sign on both. Paying a net premium can only reduce the maximum gain and enlarge the maximum loss.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A holding trades at 100.00. A manager wants a zero-cost collar and finds the 92 put quoted at 3.10, the 106 call at 1.35, the 112 call at 0.55 and the 103 call at 3.10. The call to write, and the reason the cap sits so much closer to spot than the floor, are most likely:

options.A: the 103 call, because downside puts carry higher implied volatility than upside calls.
options.B: the 112 call, because put-call parity equalises premiums at equidistant strikes.
options.C: the 106 call, because a collar's floor and cap must be equidistant from the spot price.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 88 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.A: Correct. Zero cost requires the call premium to match the 3.10 paid for the put, which only the 103 call does. Equity index implied volatility is skewed, so an out-of-the-money put costs far more than a call the same distance away, forcing the cap nearer to spot.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Put-call parity links a put and a call at the same strike, not at different strikes, and it does not imply equal premiums. The 112 call at 0.55 falls well short of funding the 3.10 put.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Nothing requires the strikes to be equidistant; they are set by whatever premiums the manager chooses to exchange. The 106 call raises only 1.35, leaving a 1.75 net debit rather than zero cost.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A manager buys a call struck at 48.00 for 3.60 and writes a call struck at 55.00 for 1.10 on the same underlying and expiration. The breakeven price and the maximum profit on the spread at expiration are most likely:

options.B: breakeven 51.60 and maximum profit 3.40.
options.C: breakeven 50.50 and maximum profit 7.00.
options.A: breakeven 50.50 and maximum profit 4.50.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 89 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.B: Incorrect. This ignores the 1.10 received on the written call. The premium collected reduces the net cost of the spread to 2.50, which lowers the breakeven and raises the maximum profit.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 7.00 is the distance between the strikes, which is the spread's gross payoff rather than its profit. The 2.50 net debit still has to be deducted from it.
explanations.A: Correct. The net debit is 3.60 - 1.10 = 2.50, so the position breaks even at 48.00 + 2.50 = 50.50 and profit is capped at (55.00 - 48.00) - 2.50 = 4.50.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: Expecting a moderate decline, a manager buys a put struck at 60.00 for 4.10 and writes a put struck at 52.00 for 1.30. The maximum profit and the breakeven price on the position at expiration are most likely:

options.A: maximum profit 5.20 and breakeven at 57.20.
options.B: maximum profit 8.00 and breakeven at 60.00.
options.C: maximum profit 3.90 and breakeven at 55.90.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 90 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.A: Correct. The net debit is 4.10 - 1.30 = 2.80. Below 52.00 the spread pays its full 8.00 width, leaving 8.00 - 2.80 = 5.20, and it breaks even at 60.00 - 2.80 = 57.20.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 8.00 is the width of the spread before cost and 60.00 is the long put's strike rather than a breakeven. Both figures omit the net premium paid to open the position.
explanations.C: Incorrect. These use only the 4.10 paid for the long put and ignore the 1.30 collected on the written put. Writing the lower-strike put is what makes the spread cheaper than an outright long put.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A manager buys a call struck at 88.00 for 2.40 and a put struck at 80.00 for 1.90 on the same underlying and expiration. The two breakeven prices for this long strangle at expiration are most likely:
origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 91 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.C: Incorrect. This charges each strike with only its own leg's premium. Both premiums are paid up front and only one leg can finish in the money, so the whole 4.30 outlay must be recovered by whichever leg pays.
explanations.A: Correct. The combined cost is 2.40 + 1.90 = 4.30, which the surviving leg must recover: the upper breakeven is 88.00 + 4.30 = 92.30 and the lower is 80.00 - 4.30 = 75.70.
explanations.B: Incorrect. These are the strikes themselves, the points at which the options begin to have intrinsic value, not the points at which the manager recovers the cost of the position.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: Each of the following institutions is using a derivative to modify a balance-sheet exposure. The pairing of exposure and tool that is most likely correct is:

options.B: a defined-benefit plan whose liabilities are longer than its assets enters a receive-fixed swap.
options.C: a bank whose liabilities reprice faster than its assets enters a receive-fixed, pay-floating swap.
options.A: a life insurer whose liabilities are longer than its assets sells long-dated bond futures.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 92 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.B: Correct. A plan with a negative duration gap loses surplus when rates fall, because liabilities gain value faster than assets. Receiving fixed on a swap adds asset-side duration and closes the gap without selling growth assets.
explanations.C: Incorrect. That bank is hurt when rates rise, since its funding cost resets before its asset yields do. Receiving fixed adds duration and worsens the exposure; the bank should pay fixed and receive floating.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Selling bond futures shortens asset duration and widens an already negative duration gap. An insurer in that position needs to lengthen assets, by buying long-dated bond futures or receiving fixed.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A manager writes a one-month at-the-money call and buys a three-month at-the-money call at the same strike on the same underlying. The view this long calendar spread most likely expresses is that:

options.B: the underlying stays near the strike near term, with implied volatility rising later.
options.C: the underlying moves sharply away from the strike before the near-dated call expires.
options.A: the underlying trends steadily higher while implied volatility falls at all maturities.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 93 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.B: Correct. The near option decays faster, so the spread earns net theta while the underlying stays near the strike, and the longer-dated leg carries more vega, so the position also gains if implied volatility rises.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A sharp move is what a long straddle or strangle wants. The calendar spread is short near-term gamma, so a large move before the front expiry is the outcome that hurts it most.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A steady trend carries the underlying away from the strike and erodes the near-term theta advantage, while falling implied volatility hurts a position that is net long vega through its back-month leg.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A manager buys an at-the-money straddle on a non-dividend-paying underlying. Immediately after execution, the position's Greek profile is best described as:

options.A: delta near zero, gamma negative, vega positive and theta positive.
options.B: delta near one, gamma positive, vega negative and theta negative.
options.C: delta near zero, gamma positive, vega positive and theta negative.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 94 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.A: Incorrect. Negative gamma with positive theta describes a short straddle, which collects premium and loses from large moves. A bought straddle carries the opposite sign on both.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A delta near one describes a long forward or a deep in-the-money call, and negative vega describes a written option. The two long legs offset in delta while reinforcing each other in vega.
explanations.C: Correct. The long call and long put have offsetting deltas near the money, but both are long convexity and long volatility, so gamma and vega are positive. Both legs also decay, which makes theta negative.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A manager has written 200 call contracts, each on 100 shares, and delta hedges with the underlying. The call delta is 0.55 when the hedge is set; the share price then rises and the delta becomes 0.65. The rebalancing trade required is most likely to:

options.A: buy 2,000 shares, adding to the hedge only after the price has already risen.
options.B: sell 2,000 shares, cutting the hedge as the written calls move into the money.
options.C: buy 13,000 shares, since the hedge is rebuilt each time from a zero position.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 95 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.A: Correct. The short position covers 20,000 shares of underlying, so the hedge is 20,000 x 0.55 = 11,000 shares initially and 20,000 x 0.65 = 13,000 after the move, a purchase of 2,000. Being short gamma, the manager is forced to buy after a rise.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Selling would be right for a long call position, whose hedge is short stock and shrinks as delta rises. A written call's delta grows with the price, so the offsetting long stock hedge must grow with it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 13,000 is the new total hedge, not the trade. The 11,000 shares already held stay in place, so only the 2,000-share increment changes hands.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A delta-hedged option position that is short gamma is rebalanced frequently over a period in which realised volatility turns out to exceed the implied volatility at which the options were written. The result for the manager is most likely:

options.A: a cumulative gain, because the written options decay steadily in the manager's favour.
options.B: a cumulative loss, because each rebalancing trade buys the underlying high and sells it low.
options.C: no net effect, since delta hedging removes the position's exposure to the underlying.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 96 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.A: Incorrect. Theta is indeed collected, but for a short gamma book theta is the payment for bearing rebalancing losses. Once realised volatility exceeds implied, those losses are larger than the decay collected.
explanations.B: Correct. A short gamma hedge must be increased after a rise and cut after a fall, so it always trades against the move. That cost scales with realised variance and exceeds the theta earned once realised volatility runs above the implied level sold.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Delta hedging neutralises the first-order price exposure at a point in time only. Second-order exposure through gamma remains, and it is exactly what turns realised volatility into profit or loss.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A manager is long a delta-hedged out-of-the-money equity index put. Over the following week the index is unchanged, but the skew steepens: implied volatility at downside strikes rises while at-the-money implied volatility is flat. The effect on the position is most likely:

options.B: a gain, because the position is long vega at the strike whose implied volatility rose.
options.C: a loss, because a steeper skew raises the cost of maintaining the delta hedge over time.
options.A: no change, because the delta hedge neutralises the position's sensitivity to volatility.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 97 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.B: Correct. Vega is strike-specific: what matters is the implied volatility of the option actually held. A long downside put gains when implied volatility at its own strike rises, even with the index and at-the-money volatility unchanged.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A steeper skew does not itself impose a hedging cost; rebalancing cost comes from realised movement in the underlying, and here the index has not moved. The skew change repriced the option, not the hedge.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A delta hedge removes the position's first-order exposure to the underlying's price, not its exposure to implied volatility. Vega, gamma and theta all survive delta hedging.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A portfolio worth 60,000,000 has a beta of 1.15 and the manager wants a beta of 0.80. Index futures with a beta of 1.00 are priced at 2,500 index points with a multiplier of 50 per point. The trade required is most likely to:

options.B: sell 168 futures contracts.
options.C: buy 168 futures contracts.
options.A: sell 384 futures contracts.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 98 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.B: Correct. One contract controls 2,500 x 50 = 125,000, so the portfolio is 60,000,000 / 125,000 = 480 contract-equivalents. The trade is (0.80 - 1.15) / 1.00 x 480 = -168, that is, sell 168 contracts.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sign follows the direction of the beta change: the target beta is below the current beta, so exposure has to be removed. Buying 168 contracts would push the beta up to roughly 1.50 instead.
explanations.A: Incorrect. 384 is 0.80 x 480, the whole exposure implied by the target beta rather than the change in beta. The futures overlay only has to bridge the 0.35 gap between the current and target beta.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A bond portfolio worth 80,000,000 has a modified duration of 4.2 and the manager wants 6.0. The futures contract to be used is priced at 100,000 per contract and has a modified duration of 7.5. The trade required is most likely to:

options.B: buy 640 futures contracts.
options.C: buy 192 futures contracts.
options.A: sell 192 futures contracts.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 99 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.B: Incorrect. 640 is (6.0 / 7.5) x 800, which sizes the entire target duration into futures instead of only the shortfall. The bonds themselves already supply 4.2 years of the 6.0 required.
explanations.C: Correct. The portfolio is 80,000,000 / 100,000 = 800 contract-equivalents, and the trade is ((6.0 - 4.2) / 7.5) x 800 = 192 contracts bought, since duration has to be added rather than removed.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Selling futures removes duration and would take the portfolio further below its target. A sale would be right only if the target duration were below the current 4.2.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A fund holds 12,000,000 in cash that policy says should sit in equities, and the manager wants the market exposure immediately while the cash is being invested. Index futures are priced at 1,600 index points with a multiplier of 250 per point. The equitising position is most likely:

options.A: short 30 futures contracts.
options.B: long 7,500 futures contracts.
options.C: long 30 futures contracts.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 100 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.A: Incorrect. A short futures position would leave the fund holding cash and a negative equity exposure, doubling the shortfall against the policy portfolio rather than closing it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 7,500 is 12,000,000 divided by the index level alone, with the 250 multiplier left out. Contract notional is the index level times the multiplier, which is 400,000 here.
explanations.C: Correct. Each contract represents 1,600 x 250 = 400,000 of index exposure, so 12,000,000 / 400,000 = 30 contracts are bought. The cash keeps earning its own return while the futures supply the equity beta.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A manager holding a portfolio of fixed-coupon bonds expects rates to rise and wants to shorten the portfolio's duration without selling any bonds. The interest rate swap position that most likely achieves this is to:

options.B: pay fixed and receive floating, converting fixed coupons to floating and cutting duration.
options.C: receive fixed and pay floating, converting floating coupons to fixed and cutting duration.
options.A: pay fixed and receive floating, which raises duration because the fixed leg is long-dated.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 101 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.B: Correct. A pay-fixed swap is economically short a fixed-rate bond and long a floating-rate note, so it carries negative duration. Overlaid on fixed-coupon holdings it converts them synthetically to floating and shortens the portfolio.
explanations.C: Incorrect. That is the mirror position, used to lengthen duration or to turn floating receipts into fixed. It has positive duration and would leave the portfolio more, not less, sensitive to a rise in rates.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The maturity of the fixed leg does not set the sign of a swap's duration; the direction of the position does. Paying fixed means being short that leg, so its long maturity works in the payer's favour as rates rise.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A manager takes exposure to an equity index through a total return swap rather than buying the constituent shares. Compared with holding the shares, the swap most likely:

options.C: delivers only the index's price return, since dividends are retained by the swap dealer.
options.A: removes market risk, because the financing leg offsets the index leg over the swap's life.
options.B: delivers the index's total return but leaves the manager with counterparty credit exposure.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 102 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.C: Incorrect. The defining feature of a total return swap is that its return leg passes through price appreciation and income together. A price-return swap is a different and narrower contract.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The financing leg is a funding cost, not a hedge, so the manager keeps the full directional exposure of the index leg. The swap changes how the exposure is funded and documented, not whether it exists.
explanations.B: Correct. The return leg pays price change plus income against a financing rate, replicating a funded holding. Because the exposure is contractual rather than owned, the manager takes on dealer credit and collateral risk and gives up voting rights.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A fund is establishing a five-year strategic allocation to an equity market and is choosing between buying the shares and rolling index futures. The strongest argument for taking the exposure physically is most likely that:

options.B: futures would require the full notional value to be posted in cash at the outset.
options.C: rolling futures repeatedly exposes the fund to roll cost and basis risk over the horizon.
options.A: a physical holding can be established faster and more cheaply than a futures position.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 103 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.B: Incorrect. Futures require initial and variation margin rather than the full notional, and that capital efficiency is one of their advantages. The case for physical rests on the durability of the exposure, not on funding.
explanations.C: Correct. A strategic multi-year exposure must be rolled many times, and each roll carries an uncertain spread and imperfect tracking of the index. A physical holding removes both, which is why synthetic exposure suits temporary or transitional needs.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The reverse is normally true: futures trade in size at lower transaction cost and settle faster than assembling a share portfolio. Speed and cost are the standard arguments for the synthetic route.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A manager has an exposure of 25,000,000 to a currency with no liquid forward market and hedges using a forward on a closely related currency. The exposure's returns have a standard deviation of 12%, the hedging currency's 15%, and their correlation is 0.80. The minimum-variance hedge ratio and notional to sell forward are most likely:

options.B: 0.80, selling 20,000,000 of the hedging currency forward.
options.C: 1.00, selling 25,000,000 of the hedging currency forward.
options.A: 0.64, selling 16,000,000 of the hedging currency forward.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 104 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.B: Incorrect. 0.80 is the correlation on its own. The minimum-variance ratio is a regression slope, so relative volatilities matter too, and here the proxy is the more volatile of the pair, which scales the ratio down.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A unit hedge ratio matches notionals one for one and is appropriate only for a direct hedge of the same currency. Applied to a cross hedge it over-hedges, because the proxy moves more than the exposure.
explanations.A: Correct. The minimum-variance hedge ratio is the correlation times the ratio of standard deviations: 0.80 x (12 / 15) = 0.64, so 25,000,000 x 0.64 = 16,000,000 is sold. It is estimated from past data and drifts as that relationship changes.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A domestic-currency investor holds a foreign asset that returns 7.0% over one year measured in the foreign currency. Over the same year the spot rate moves from 1.2500 to 1.2100 units of domestic currency per unit of foreign currency. The unhedged return in domestic-currency terms is closest to:
origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 105 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.A: Correct. The currency return is 1.2100 / 1.2500 - 1 = -3.2%, and the two returns compound: (1.07)(1 - 0.032) - 1 = 3.58%. The currency loss applies to the grown asset value, not only to the original principal.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 3.80% simply adds 7.0% and -3.2%, dropping the cross-product term. The additive approximation is close but understates the currency drag whenever the asset itself has gained.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 10.20% adds the size of the currency move to the asset return with the wrong sign. The foreign currency has weakened against the domestic currency here, so it detracts from the return.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: Spot is 1.2500 units of domestic currency per unit of foreign currency and the one-year forward is 1.2250. A domestic-currency manager hedges foreign assets by selling the foreign currency forward, and the spot rate is unchanged a year later. The outcome is most likely:

options.A: a roll yield of about +2.0%, because a short forward position earns the forward premium.
options.B: a roll yield of about -2.0%, because the foreign currency trades at a forward discount.
options.C: a roll yield of about zero, because covered interest parity removes any gain or loss.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 106 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.A: Incorrect. There is no premium to earn: the forward sits below spot, so the foreign currency is at a discount, and a seller of a currency at a discount gives up value rather than collecting it.
explanations.B: Correct. The manager contracts to sell at 1.2250 and, with spot unchanged, gives up 0.0250 against a spot of 1.2500, or 2.0%. A forward discount on the foreign currency, which arises when its interest rate is the higher one, makes hedging costly.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Covered interest parity is what creates the discount, by tying the forward to the interest rate differential; it does not neutralise it. Parity rules out arbitrage, not the realised cost of carrying a hedge.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: An investment committee is setting strategic currency hedge ratios for a portfolio holding both foreign bonds and foreign equities. The argument that most strongly supports hedging the bond sleeve more fully than the equity sleeve is that:

options.B: currency volatility is large relative to bond return volatility, so it dominates that sleeve's risk.
options.C: currency returns are expected to be positive over the long run for bond investors but negative for equity investors.
options.A: forward contracts on the currencies of bond markets are systematically cheaper than those on equity markets.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 107 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.B: Correct. Exchange rate volatility is typically of a similar order to equity volatility but several times that of a bond portfolio, so unhedged currency dominates the risk of a foreign bond sleeve while adding proportionately less to a foreign equity sleeve.
explanations.C: Incorrect. No such asset-class-specific expected currency return exists; the same exchange rate applies to both sleeves. The case for a higher bond hedge ratio rests on risk contribution, not on an expected return from currency.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Forward pricing follows the interest rate differential of the currency pair, not the asset class of the underlying holding. The same currency costs the same to hedge for a bond position and an equity position.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A committee will tolerate modest deviation from its strategic hedge ratio so that the overlay manager can avoid a hedge that has become expensive, but it does not want currency treated as a separate source of return. The mandate best suited to this is:

options.A: passive hedging, with the hedge ratio held mechanically at the strategic level.
options.B: discretionary hedging, with limited deviation permitted around the strategic ratio.
options.C: active currency management, with currency run as an independent alpha source.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 108 | Derivatives and Risk Management

explanations.A: Incorrect. A passive mandate rebalances back to the benchmark hedge ratio regardless of cost and permits no view at all, so it cannot act on an expensive hedge. Its objective is to minimise tracking error against the benchmark.
explanations.B: Correct. A discretionary overlay keeps risk reduction as the objective but allows bounded deviation from the strategic ratio to exploit clear opportunities, which is exactly the balance the committee has described.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An active mandate treats currency as a return source in its own right and may take positions unrelated to the underlying exposures, including in currencies the portfolio does not hold. The committee has ruled that out.

subject: Derivatives and Risk Management

stem: A pension consultant is running a search for an emerging-markets equity manager. One candidate firm offers to fly the consultant's due-diligence team to its Singapore office on the firm's corporate aircraft and to host the team for two nights, arguing that a visit is the only way to meet the whole investment team. The response most consistent with Standard I(B) Independence and Objectivity is for the consultant to:

options.B: accept the flight and the accommodation, provided the arrangement is disclosed to the search client in the final report.
options.C: make the trip but pay the team's own travel and lodging costs, keeping only the office visit itself.
options.A: decline the visit altogether, because an on-site meeting with a firm competing for the mandate compromises the search.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 109 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.B: Incorrect. Disclosure does not cure the problem here. Accepting travel and hospitality from a firm still competing for the mandate creates the appearance of dependence the standard exists to prevent, and it does so before the recommendation is made.
explanations.C: Correct. Standard I(B) requires members to protect their independence and to avoid situations that could reasonably be seen to compromise it. Paying the team's own way removes the benefit conferred by the candidate while preserving the on-site diligence the search needs.
explanations.A: Incorrect. On-site diligence is good practice, not a conflict; the standard governs who pays for it, not whether it happens. Refusing to visit would weaken the search rather than protect its objectivity.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: Completing an institutional manager questionnaire, the head of a boutique's investment team describes the firm's risk model as 'developed in house' when it is a commercial vendor model with the firm's own factor overlay, and reports firm assets under management on a basis that folds in accounts the firm advises without discretion. Under Standard I(C) Misrepresentation, these two entries are best described as:

options.C: acceptable, because a questionnaire is a marketing document rather than a communication with a client.
options.A: a misrepresentation only in the assets figure, since a model's authorship is a matter of characterisation.
options.B: both misrepresentations, because each states something about the firm that is untrue as written.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 110 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.C: Incorrect. The standard covers all communications about the firm and its services, and an RFP or manager questionnaire is precisely the document an institutional client relies on when selecting a manager.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Who built a model is a verifiable fact, not a characterisation. Adding a proprietary overlay to a licensed model does not make the firm the model's developer, although the firm may fairly describe the overlay as its own work.
explanations.B: Correct. Standard I(C) prohibits any untrue statement of material fact in a communication about the firm's services. Calling a vendor model in-house and inflating assets under management with non-discretionary advisory relationships both overstate the firm as written.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A multi-strategy firm's private-credit team joins a lender committee and learns that a listed issuer will shortly announce a distressed restructuring. A portfolio manager on the firm's long-only equity desk holds the issuer's shares in several client accounts and knows nothing of the committee's work. The firm's most appropriate action is to:

options.C: instruct the equity desk to sell the position at once, because selling on bad news disadvantages no one.
options.A: place the issuer on a restricted list, so that no desk deals in the security until the news is public.
options.B: cross the equity portfolio manager over the wall, leaving him free to trade on his own prior research.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 111 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.C: Incorrect. The prohibition applies to selling exactly as it applies to buying: the buyer on the other side is disadvantaged in the same way. Liquidating ahead of the announcement would be acting on the information.
explanations.A: Correct. Standard II(A) prohibits acting, or causing others to act, on material nonpublic information. A restricted list stops the firm dealing in the security across every desk while the information is held, and is the usual control when one part of a firm becomes an insider.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Crossing the wall means bringing someone inside the information and restricting them, not releasing them to trade. Once crossed, the portfolio manager would be barred from dealing in the security rather than permitted to.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A firm that runs both an investment-banking arm and a discretionary asset-management arm is reviewing its information barrier. Which feature is most essential if the barrier is to serve the purpose of Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information?

options.A: Physical separation of the two arms' offices, so that employees of one arm never encounter those of the other.
options.B: Control of information flow on a need-to-know basis, with a documented procedure for crossing the barrier.
options.C: A standing prohibition on the asset-management arm holding any security the banking arm has ever advised on.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 112 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.A: Incorrect. Physical separation supports a barrier but is not one. Information travels by e-mail, shared systems and committee papers, and staff of the two arms legitimately meet on firm-wide matters.
explanations.B: Correct. The standard expects a firm to control material nonpublic information so that it reaches only those who need it, with a recorded process for bringing someone across and restricting them once crossed. That control, together with review of trading in affected securities, is what makes a barrier real.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A permanent ban on every security the banking arm has touched is not required and would penalise the asset-management clients. The duty is to restrict dealing while material nonpublic information is held, not indefinitely.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A manager runs the assets of a corporate defined-benefit pension plan. The sponsor's treasurer asks her to move a large part of the portfolio into higher-risk assets, explaining that a higher assumed return would let the sponsor reduce this year's contribution. Under Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, the manager should most likely:

options.A: comply, because the sponsor engaged her and is the party whose instructions govern this account.
options.B: comply if the shift stays inside the policy ranges, since the sponsor is knowingly accepting the risk.
options.C: decline, because her duty runs to the plan's participants and beneficiaries rather than to the sponsor.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 113 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.A: Incorrect. The party that hires and pays the manager is not necessarily the client for the purposes of the duty of loyalty. In a defined-benefit plan the assets are held in trust, and the beneficiaries' interest governs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Staying inside the policy ranges does not legitimise the reason for the trade. The manager would be taking additional risk on the beneficiaries' behalf to obtain an accounting benefit for the sponsor, and the sponsor's willingness to accept that risk does not make it the party she must serve.
explanations.C: Correct. Under Standard III(A) the client of a pension manager is the plan's participants and beneficiaries, not the sponsor's management. An instruction whose purpose is to lower the sponsor's contribution serves the sponsor at the beneficiaries' expense.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A firm places a single block order on behalf of twelve client accounts and receives a partial fill executed at several different prices. Which allocation of that fill is most consistent with Standard III(B) Fair Dealing?

options.B: Every participating account receives the same average execution price and a pro rata share of the fill.
options.C: Accounts are filled in the order in which their portfolio managers submitted the underlying instructions.
options.A: Accounts furthest from their target weight are filled first, so that tracking error is reduced fastest.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 114 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.B: Correct. Standard III(B) requires that all clients participating in a block be treated fairly. Averaging the price across the fill and allocating pro rata means no account is advantaged by the sequence in which the individual executions happened to arrive.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Filling in order of instruction rewards whichever portfolio manager acted first that morning and systematically disadvantages the others. Order of arrival is a queue rule for separate orders, not an allocation rule for one block.
explanations.A: Incorrect. This is a portfolio-construction rationale rather than a fair-dealing one, and it lets the firm choose which clients receive a scarce fill. What the standard looks for is a written allocation policy applied consistently.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A private client's investment policy statement prohibits the use of leverage. Her manager identifies a levered closed-end fund that he believes would materially improve the portfolio's risk-adjusted return. Under Standard III(C) Suitability, the manager should most likely:

options.C: take a small position, since a holding too small to change the portfolio's risk profile is not leverage.
options.A: not buy it, and raise the constraint with the client so the policy statement can be formally amended.
options.B: buy it, because suitability is judged against the client's objectives rather than against her constraints.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 115 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.C: Incorrect. A constraint binds whatever the size of the position, and the standard carries no materiality exemption. A small breach also establishes that the policy statement is advisory rather than binding.
explanations.A: Correct. Standard III(C) requires the manager to act in line with the written policy statement. A good idea is not made suitable by being good; the route is to discuss the constraint with the client and amend the document before acting.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Suitability is judged against objectives and constraints together. Constraints are what translate a client's circumstances, liquidity needs and preferences into limits, and they bind the manager just as objectives do.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A private client's portfolio, managed against a written policy statement, is to receive a small allocation to a high-volatility biotechnology fund. In judging whether that purchase is suitable, Standard III(C) Suitability requires the manager to assess the holding:

options.C: on its own risk and return characteristics, because every holding must independently meet the mandate.
options.A: against the volatility limit of the strategy sleeve it will sit in, which is where the risk budget is set.
options.B: in the context of the client's total portfolio, so its effect on overall risk and return is what counts.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 116 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.C: Incorrect. Judging each holding in isolation would exclude diversifying positions that improve the portfolio and admit correlated ones that do not. The standard asks about the effect on the whole.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A sleeve limit is an internal risk-budgeting device — useful, but not the test the standard sets. The client's total portfolio, not the sleeve, is the reference point for suitability.
explanations.B: Correct. Standard III(C) requires a manager with discretion to judge a purchase in the context of the client's total portfolio. A volatile holding can lower total risk if it diversifies, and a low-volatility one can raise it if it concentrates an existing exposure.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: Preparing a presentation for a prospective institutional client, a manager builds the record for its value-equity strategy from the accounts that still follow the strategy today; three accounts that terminated during the period shown are left out. That presentation is best described as:

options.B: acceptable, because a composite is meant to describe how the strategy is currently being managed.
options.C: misleading, because dropping the accounts that left removes the strategy's worst outcomes from the record.
options.A: acceptable if the departures were client-initiated, since those results reflect the clients' own decisions.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 117 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.B: Incorrect. A record of past performance describes what happened, not what the current book looks like. Showing only surviving accounts answers a question the prospective client is not asking.
explanations.C: Correct. Standard III(D) prohibits presentations that misstate performance. Excluding terminated accounts leaves a survivorship-biased record — accounts that leave are disproportionately the disappointing ones — and overstates what the strategy actually delivered.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Why an account left does not change the fact that its returns were produced by this strategy in the period shown. Returns earned while the account was under management belong in the record.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A wealth manager advises a widowed client and, separately, her adult son, who is also a client of the firm. The son telephones to ask what his mother's portfolio is worth, saying he needs the figure for the family's estate planning. Absent any instruction from the mother, the manager should most likely:

options.C: give the figure, because both parties are clients of the firm and the purpose is a family matter.
options.A: give a range rather than an exact value, since an approximation does not disclose the account itself.
options.B: decline, and offer to ask his mother whether she wishes to authorise the disclosure to her son.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 118 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.C: Incorrect. Confidentiality runs account by account, not household by household. A shared adviser and a family purpose do not create consent, and the mother may have reasons of her own for not wanting the figure known.
explanations.A: Incorrect. An approximate figure is still the client's information, and a range close enough to be useful is close enough to be a disclosure. The size of the leak does not change its character.
explanations.B: Correct. Standard III(E) requires a member to keep information about current, former and prospective clients confidential. Being a client of the same firm gives the son no claim on his mother's information; her authorisation is what would permit the disclosure.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A retired client with no other significant assets instructs his adviser to move his entire portfolio into the shares of his former employer — a decision that is lawful and that the client is entitled to make, but that conflicts with the objectives in his policy statement. The adviser's most appropriate response is to:

options.B: explain how the concentration conflicts with his stated objectives, document the discussion, and act only on a confirmed instruction.
options.C: carry out the instruction without further comment, because a client's express written direction overrides the adviser's own view of the portfolio.
options.A: refuse the instruction and resign the relationship, since carrying out a trade the adviser regards as unsuitable is itself a violation.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 119 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.B: Correct. The instruction is lawful and the client may give it, so the adviser's obligation is to make sure it is an informed decision: set out what concentrating a sole retirement asset in one employer's shares does to the objectives already agreed, record the conversation, and act only once the client confirms.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Executing in silence abandons the advisory duty the client is paying for. A client's right to direct the account does not relieve the adviser of the obligation to explain the consequences before it is carried out.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Following an informed, lawful client direction is not a violation, and resigning at the first disagreement serves nobody. Resignation belongs where the client insists on something unlawful or the adviser can no longer act properly.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A portfolio manager resigns to found her own firm. Before her last day she copies the employer's client contact list and the monthly performance files for the composite she ran, intending to use both at the new firm. Under Standard IV(A) Loyalty, her position is best described as follows:

options.A: both files belong to her, because she generated the returns and personally sourced most of the client relationships.
options.B: both files belong to the employer; she may cite the record later only with attribution and its permission to use the data.
options.C: the contact list may be taken because client names are public, but the performance files remain the employer's property.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 120 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.A: Incorrect. Producing the returns and sourcing the relationships does not transfer ownership of the employer's records; the work was done for the employer and with its resources. What she carries in her memory is hers, the files are not.
explanations.B: Correct. Under Standard IV(A), records created during employment — client lists and performance files alike — are the employer's property, and copying them before departure is misappropriation. She may later refer to the record she produced, attributed to the former firm and with its permission to use the underlying data.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A compiled client list is the employer's property even where individual names could in principle be found elsewhere, because the value lies in the compilation. Public availability of a fact does not release her from the duty of loyalty.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: The head of a firm's trading desk is told by compliance that the desk's exception reports have not been produced for four months following a system change, and that nobody has reviewed the desk's trade allocations in that time. Under Standard IV(C) Responsibilities of Supervisors, the desk head should most likely:

options.C: leave restoration of the reports to compliance, because designing surveillance systems is the compliance function's role.
options.A: wait for a specific allegation of misallocation before reviewing, so as not to imply distrust of the desk's own traders.
options.B: act at once to restore the review and examine the unreviewed period, since a supervisor must ensure the system works.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 121 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.C: Incorrect. Compliance builds and maintains the systems, but delegating the task does not delegate the responsibility; the supervisor remains answerable for the desk. His knowledge of the gap is what triggers the duty to act.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Supervision is a preventive obligation rather than a response to complaints. Waiting for an allegation is the very failure the standard describes, and the absence of surveillance is the reason no allegation would surface.
explanations.B: Correct. Standard IV(C) makes a supervisor responsible for ensuring that compliance procedures actually operate, not merely that they exist on paper. Once he knows the review has lapsed he must restore it and look back over the period that went unchecked.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
