stem: A fund-of-funds analyst recommends allocating to an external long/short manager after reading its pitch book, its audited financial statements and two favourable consultant write-ups. He has not examined the manager's risk controls or how its reported returns are produced. Under Standard V(A) Diligence and Reasonable Basis, his recommendation is best described as:

options.B: lacking a reasonable basis, because he must judge the soundness of the process that produced the returns.
options.C: supported, because audited statements and independent consultant coverage amount to third-party verification.
options.A: supported, since responsibility for the external manager's risk controls rests with that manager's own compliance.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 122 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.B: Correct. Standard V(A) requires a reasonable and adequate basis supported by appropriate research. Where the recommendation is to hire someone else to invest, diligence means examining how the returns were generated and controlled, not merely that they were reported and audited.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An audit addresses the financial statements, not the soundness of an investment process, and consultant write-ups are third-party opinions the analyst still has to evaluate. Adopting others' conclusions is not the same as having a basis.
explanations.A: Incorrect. The external manager is responsible for its own controls, but the analyst is responsible for the recommendation to place client money with it. Delegating the investment does not delegate the duty of diligence.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A quarterly letter to clients reads: 'The portfolio returned 6.2% in the quarter, and its high-conviction holdings will continue to outpace the index over the coming year.' Under Standard V(B) Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients, the principal defect in that sentence is that it:

options.C: quotes a return figure without saying whether management fees have already been deducted from it.
options.A: presents a forecast in the same register as a reported return, so that opinion reads to the client as fact.
options.B: refers to 'high-conviction' holdings without defining how that subset of the portfolio is identified.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 123 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.C: Incorrect. Whether the figure is gross or net matters and ought to be stated, but that is a completeness point about the number rather than the fact-versus-opinion failure the sentence displays.
explanations.A: Correct. Standard V(B) requires members to distinguish fact from opinion. The realised return is a fact; continued outperformance is a forecast, and joining the two in one sentence invites the client to read both as reported results.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Defining a subset of holdings is a useful disclosure about the process, not the defect at issue. The sentence would still blur fact and forecast even with the term fully defined.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A systematic equity manager replaces the momentum signal at the core of its process with a machine-learning model trained on the same data, leaving the strategy's stated objective and benchmark unchanged. With respect to its existing clients, the firm should most likely:

options.C: disclose the change at the next annual review, since neither the objective nor the benchmark has moved.
options.A: treat the change as proprietary, as revealing model detail would erode the edge the clients are paying for.
options.B: disclose the change promptly, because clients selected the process as well as the stated objective.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 124 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.C: Incorrect. An unchanged objective and benchmark say nothing about how the returns will now be generated. Holding the news until an annual review leaves clients invested in a strategy that is no longer the one they evaluated.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Saying that the process has changed, and in general terms how, does not require publishing the model's parameters. Proprietary detail may be withheld; the fact of a material change may not.
explanations.B: Correct. Standard V(B) requires prompt disclosure of a material change to the investment process. Clients chose the manager partly for how it invests, and replacing the core signal changes the thing they bought even though the label is the same.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A portfolio manager wishes to buy, for his own account, a small-cap stock that he is about to begin accumulating for several client portfolios over the coming weeks. Under Standard VI(B) Priority of Transactions, he may most likely:

options.B: buy for his own account only once the client orders are executed or the accumulation programme is complete.
options.C: buy alongside the first client order, provided every participating account receives the same average price.
options.A: buy at any point, provided the personal trade is reported to compliance within the firm's reporting window.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 125 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.B: Correct. Standard VI(B) requires transactions for clients to take precedence over transactions in which a member is a beneficial owner. Buying ahead of an accumulation programme in a thin small-cap lets the manager's own purchase be improved by the client buying that follows.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sharing an average price still places the manager's capital alongside clients' in a scarce, price-sensitive situation and consumes liquidity that would otherwise be theirs. Priority means clients first, not clients equally.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Pre-clearance and reporting are how a firm monitors personal trading; they do not authorise a trade that runs ahead of a client order. Reporting the trade afterwards cures nothing.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: An independent financial planner agrees to receive a continuing share of the management fee for every client she refers to a discretionary asset manager. Under Standard VI(C) Referral Fees, she must most likely disclose:

options.C: the arrangement to her professional body, which maintains the register of such compensation agreements.
options.A: the arrangement, including what it is worth, to each referred client before that client engages the manager.
options.B: the arrangement whenever a client asks how she is paid, since unsolicited fee detail tends to confuse clients.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 126 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.C: Incorrect. Any registration or regulatory filing the arrangement attracts is a separate legal obligation. The disclosure this standard requires runs to the client and to the member's employer, not to a professional body.
explanations.A: Correct. Standard VI(C) requires disclosure of referral compensation, including its nature and value, so that the referred client can judge how far the recommendation is influenced by the payment. It must come before the client engages, while it can still affect the decision.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Waiting to be asked leaves the client deciding without the one fact that bears on the adviser's motive. The duty is to volunteer the arrangement, not merely to answer honestly if the question happens to be put.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: An institutional client instructs its manager to place a fixed share of the portfolio's trades with a broker that supplies the client with performance-attribution reporting. The manager finds that this broker's execution is consistently worse than the alternatives available. The manager should most likely:

options.B: disregard the instruction wherever execution would suffer, since best execution outranks a client preference.
options.C: apply the research obtained to all client accounts, since soft-dollar benefits accrue to the firm's clients generally.
options.A: tell the client that the direction may be costing it best execution, and record its decision to continue.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 127 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.B: Incorrect. The commissions are the client's, and a client is entitled to direct its own brokerage even at a cost to execution quality. Quietly overriding the instruction substitutes the manager's judgement for a decision the client is allowed to make.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Benefits bought with one client's directed commissions should serve that client; spreading them across the book has the directing client subsidising the others. Directed-brokerage benefits are not a firm resource to redistribute.
explanations.A: Correct. A client may direct its brokerage and the manager must follow the instruction, but the duty of loyalty requires telling the client that the direction may be reducing execution quality and documenting that the client chose to continue once informed.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: An asset management firm announces that it has adopted the CFA Institute Asset Manager Code. That announcement is best described as a commitment that:

options.A: the firm as a whole complies with every provision of the Code, which it may not adopt selectively.
options.B: each of the firm's charterholders will observe the Code in addition to the Code and Standards.
options.C: CFA Institute has reviewed the firm's policies and certified them as compliant with the Code.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 128 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.A: Correct. The Asset Manager Code is a voluntary, firm-level code adopted whole — a manager cannot claim compliance with parts of it. Adoption commits the firm to its general principles of conduct and to its provisions covering loyalty to clients, the investment process and actions, trading, risk management and compliance, performance and valuation, and disclosures.
explanations.B: Incorrect. That describes the Code and Standards, which bind individual members and candidates. The Asset Manager Code operates at the level of the firm and governs it whether or not its staff hold the charter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. CFA Institute does not review, verify or certify a firm's compliance. A firm claiming compliance notifies CFA Institute, and responsibility for the accuracy of the claim stays with the firm.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A prospective client is comparing the equity records of three managers and asks why each presents composite returns rather than the record of a representative account. Which statement about composites under the GIPS standards is most accurate?

options.B: A composite groups a firm's largest portfolios, so that the record reflects its most significant clients.
options.C: A composite groups portfolios by mandate or strategy, so a firm cannot show only its best accounts.
options.A: A composite groups portfolios by inception date, so that every period shown is a like-for-like span.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 129 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.B: Incorrect. Size does not define a composite, and grouping by the largest accounts would reintroduce exactly the selection the standards exist to prevent. Every actual, fee-paying, discretionary portfolio must sit in at least one composite.
explanations.C: Correct. A composite is all portfolios managed to a given mandate, objective or strategy, which is what stops a firm presenting a hand-picked representative account. That is also why a prospective client asks for GIPS-compliant figures: they can be compared across managers on the same basis.
explanations.A: Incorrect. Inception date affects how long a portfolio has been in a composite, not which composite it belongs to. Membership follows the strategy the portfolio is managed to.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A firm claiming compliance with the GIPS standards is deciding what may go into its composites. Which treatment is most accurate?

options.A: A carve-out may be included without cash allocated to it; non-discretionary portfolios form their own composite.
options.B: A carve-out may never be included in a composite; non-discretionary portfolios must be included with a note.
options.C: A carve-out may be included only if cash has been allocated to it; non-discretionary portfolios are excluded.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 130 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.A: Incorrect. A carve-out with no cash allocated overstates what a standalone portfolio in that strategy would have earned, so it cannot be treated as a portfolio. Non-discretionary portfolios are not given a composite of their own either — they are left out of composites altogether.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Carve-outs are not prohibited; once cash is allocated they may be included. Attaching a note to a non-discretionary portfolio does not make its return attributable to the firm's investment decisions.
explanations.C: Correct. A carve-out can be treated as a portfolio only once cash is allocated to it, because a return carrying no cash drag is not the return a client would actually have received. Non-discretionary portfolios are excluded because the firm did not control the decisions that produced the result.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A manager tells a prospective client that its claim of compliance with the GIPS standards has been verified. What that verification covers is best described as:

options.A: the firm's composite construction and its policies for calculating and presenting performance, firm-wide.
options.B: the accuracy of the figures in each composite report the firm distributes to prospective clients.
options.C: the firm's investment process, confirming that portfolios were managed as the composite describes.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 131 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.A: Correct. Verification is a firm-wide engagement by an independent third party, testing whether the firm has complied with the composite construction requirements on a firm-wide basis and whether its policies and procedures are designed to calculate and present performance in compliance with the standards.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Testing the figures in a specific composite is a performance examination — a separate, additional engagement. Verification on its own does not attest to the accuracy of any individual composite report.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Verification addresses performance measurement and presentation, not how the portfolios were actually invested. Whether the manager followed the process it describes is a due-diligence question rather than a verification one.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards

stem: A corporate bond held in a GIPS-compliant composite did not trade on the valuation date, although bonds of the same issuer and maturity did trade that day. Under the fair-value hierarchy, the manager should most likely value the holding using:

options.B: the bond's own last traded price, however stale, because an actual transaction is objective evidence.
options.C: quoted prices for those similar bonds, since observable market data outranks an internal estimate.
options.A: her own discounted-cash-flow model, because only that captures this particular bond's exact terms.

origin: CFA Level III | Practice item 132 | Ethical and Professional Standards

explanations.B: Incorrect. A stale price is objective but no longer reflects fair value on the valuation date. The hierarchy asks for the best current evidence of value, not for the most recent transaction in that particular security.
explanations.C: Correct. The fair-value hierarchy gives priority to objective, observable market data. With no quoted price for the identical bond on the date, quoted prices for similar investments that did trade rank ahead of any price the manager models herself.
explanations.A: Incorrect. A manager's own model rests on subjective, unobservable inputs and sits at the bottom of the hierarchy — and it is produced by the party whose reported performance depends on the answer. It is the fallback for when observable data is unavailable.

subject: Ethical and Professional Standards
